title: Shaheedi Jor Mela
hookLine: in December Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib to remember the younger Sahibzade

lines: A TOWN FULL OF PEOPLE IN DECEMBER.
cards: The last week of December. Much of the world is between holidays, but the roads around a Punjab town called Fatehgarh Sahib fill with people.
Huge crowds come, on foot, in buses, on tractor trolleys carrying half a village. It isn't a celebration. Nobody's dressed for a party, there are no fireworks, and the mood is quiet, almost hushed.
They've come to remember two little boys and their grandmother.

teach.b: The gathering is the Shaheedi Jor Mela. Shaheedi means of the martyrs; jor mela is a gathering, a coming together.

On day ninety you heard what it remembers. Tradition says the Guru's mother, Mata Gujri, and his two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were handed over to the governor of Sirhind and held in a cold tower.

teach.h: THE WALL, THE TOWER, THE GOLD.
teach.b: The boys refused to give up their faith and were bricked into a wall and put to death, and their grandmother died in the tower. Today is about the place, and the days.
The town is now called Fatehgarh Sahib, after the younger boy. Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib stands where tradition places the wall. Close by, Gurdwara Thanda Burj keeps the memory of the cold tower.
A little way off is Gurdwara Jyoti Sarup, on ground that a merchant named Todar Mal, tradition says, bought for their cremation by covering it with gold coins.
The mela moves between these places over several days at the end of December: unbroken readings, kirtan in tents, langar along the roads, and a long procession.
Far from Fatehgarh, some families keep the whole week in mourning at home: no parties, no sweets, a mattress on the floor instead of a bed.
One more name is honored in these days: Malerkotla, whose Nawab, Sher Muhammad Khan, protested in open court that children must not be punished.
People sometimes say the boys were too young to understand what they were choosing. Sikhs remember it the other way: small, and yet they would not bend.

how: In late December, Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib for the Shaheedi Jor Mela with kirtan, prayers, langar and a procession; some families observe the week in mourning, sleeping on the floor and keeping celebrations away.

o: a holy man who has given up worldly life
a warrior who wins a great battle for his people
a martyr, one who gives their life for the faith

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: the ground Todar Mal bought with gold

s: the Shaheedi Jor Mela is a festive fair
it's kept in mourning: some families sleep on the floor and keep the week quiet.
a Muslim nawab spoke up for the boys
the Nawab of Malerkotla, Sher Muhammad Khan, protested that children must not be punished.
Fatehgarh is named for the older boy
it's named for Fateh Singh, the younger.

games.q: it's the last week of December, and you're in a Sikh home far from Fatehgarh. how is the week kept?
o: quietly: no celebrations, perhaps a mattress on the floor.
no differently from any other week.
games.why: some families keep the week in mourning, in memory of a grandmother and two boys in a cold tower.

practice: Sit still and think of the two boys and their grandmother; you don't need to picture the wall, just them together, her hand resting on each small head.
Then let the circle widen to children anywhere who are carrying things too heavy for them.
If you pray, hold them all in Waheguru; if you don't, simply keep them company in the silence, the way you'd sit beside someone who is grieving.

wordCard.voice: Shaheed. Martyr: the word behind the Shaheedi Jor Mela, the gathering at Fatehgarh Sahib each December to remember the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the martyrs' gathering. shaheed comes into Punjabi from Arabic, through Persian.

carryVoice: Your line: small, and unbending. The week behind you held an unbroken reading, a Guru's birthday, cool water, lamps for the freed, strength in joy, and coming back. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 5, life of Guru Gobind Singh (Sirhind)
